name: Oluseyi Abiodun Makinde
provenance: AI-assisted web research (Claude), pending human review

partyHistory.period: elected governor on the PDP platform in 2019 and 2023; still described as a PDP governor in May 2026
2026 to date (presidential candidate under a PDP-APM memorandum of understanding)

professional: Founder of Makon Engineering and Technical Services (1997), later Makon Group (oil and gas, power); resigned in 2018 according to a 2024 speaker profile

career.title: Oil and gas engineering
career.description: Worked for about five years with international oil and gas companies after graduating. Sources differ on whether his Shell experience was an industrial attachment or post-graduation employment.

career.title: Founder, Makon Engineering and Technical Services / Makon Group
career.description: Founded an engineering services company that grew into a group working in oil and gas and power generation and distribution. A 2024 profile says he resigned in 2018 to contest the governorship.

career.title: Governor of Oyo State
career.description: Elected in March 2019 on the PDP platform and re-elected in March 2023. The second term ends in May 2027.

career.title: Presidential declaration and APM nomination
career.description: Declared for the presidency on 14 May 2026 at a joint PDP-APM rally in Ibadan after signing a PDP-APM memorandum of understanding; received the APM certificate of return after the party's Ibadan primary (reported 30 May 2026).

career.title: Running mate named
career.description: Named Lawal Musa Daura, a former Director-General of the State Security Service, as running mate. Daura had left the ADC four days earlier.

career.title: Manifesto launch
career.description: Unveiled 'The Reset Agenda', a four-pillar programme (economy, security, education, socio-political reset) with three years of principal commitments and a fourth year of consolidation.

elections.result: Won: 515,621 votes to 357,982 for Adebayo Adelabu (APC), per INEC as reported by Channels; the tribunal later upheld the result.
Re-elected: 563,756 votes to 256,685 for Teslim Folarin (APC), declared 19 March 2023.
Nominated; all state chapters and the FCT chapter endorsed him. No vote count was reported.
Listed as the APM candidate on INEC's final list. The election is pending.

economy.summary: As governor he grew Oyo's own revenue, but the state still relies mostly on federal transfers and recorded high food inflation. His presidential economic plan is detailed on refineries, fuel pricing and fiscal targets, but its costs are not stated.
economy.analysis:
As governor, Makinde controls only state-level levers: taxes and levies, agriculture programmes, investment promotion and state spending. Inflation, the exchange rate, fuel pricing and federal taxes belong to the CBN and the federal government. FIRS reported that Oyo's internally generated revenue rose to ₦65.28 billion in 2024 from ₦52.74 billion in 2023, after ₦62.24 billion in 2022 (FACT). The FIRS chairman put cumulative growth since 2019 at 145.5 per cent. Even so, a Premium Times analysis of his manifesto notes that federal allocations still made up 86.7 per cent of Oyo's 2024 recurrent revenue, and that Oyo recorded 34.41 per cent year-on-year food inflation in March 2025 (FACT). That was the period of national fuel-subsidy removal and naira devaluation, which pushed prices up in every state.

For the presidency, he proposes independent refinery assessments within six months and a decision on each refinery within 12 months. He also proposes a Domestic Energy Value Credit that would pay households a share of crude value without fixing pump prices, preserved CBN independence with a published inflation target, and no preferential FX windows (PROMISE). His plan names Oyo's Fasola agribusiness hub as a model. ANALYSIS: the plan sets targets and deadlines, but the press coverage reviewed gives no cost estimate for the energy credit and no financing for priority road corridors beyond redirecting existing spending.
strengths: Documented IGR growth over his tenure, reported by the federal tax authority
Manifesto commits to measurable fiscal and refinery milestones with deadlines
limitations: Oyo remained heavily dependent on federal allocations
State food inflation was high in 2025, though driven largely by national factors
Cost of the proposed Domestic Energy Value Credit is not published in the sources reviewed
unknowns: Independent data on Oyo GDP or poverty change during his tenure

metrics.label: Federal allocations share of recurrent revenue

security.summary: He governed through serious insecurity, including the May 2026 mass school abduction in Oriire, using Amotekun and coordination with federal forces. He proposes phased state police within three years.
security.analysis:
Nigeria's police and armed forces are federal, so a governor's security role is limited to funding, coordination and the state-backed Western Nigeria Security Network (Amotekun). In May 2026, gunmen attacked schools in Oriire Local Government Area. Makinde said 39 pupils and seven teachers were abducted and one teacher was killed, though another report gave a lower count (DISPUTED). The Defence Headquarters attributed the attack to a Boko Haram faction. At the end of May, the captives had not been released. Makinde said he was holding twice-daily security meetings, that nearly 200 Amotekun operatives had died since the corps was formed, and that he was willing to negotiate (RECORD/FACT). The sources reviewed do not report the outcome of the abduction.

For the presidency, he chose a former SSS Director-General as running mate, explicitly for security reasons. His manifesto sets out a phased state police plan: a legal framework in year one, training and oversight in year two, and compliant services by the end of year three. It adds lead-agency rules for threats, community recovery plans, and investigations into police extortion and extrajudicial killings (PROMISE). ANALYSIS: state police require a constitutional amendment, so the timeline depends on the National Assembly and state assemblies. No independent statistics on Oyo crime trends over his tenure were found.
strengths: Specific, phased state-police timeline
Manifesto includes human-rights accountability commitments
limitations: Mass school abduction occurred in his state in 2026 and its outcome is not documented in sources reviewed
Amotekun capacity constraints acknowledged by the governor himself
unknowns: Oyo kidnapping and homicide trend data 2019-2026

education.summary: He abolished secondary-school fees in 2019 and approved teacher recruitment, but public schools faced teacher shortages. He proposes national foundational-learning targets.
education.analysis:
On taking office on 29 May 2019, Makinde scrapped the ₦3,000 levy paid by Oyo secondary-school students, fulfilling a campaign promise (RECORD). Other levies followed. Critics noted that external examination fees such as WAEC and NECO were not covered, and the government replied that it had never promised to pay them. The resulting rise in public-school enrolment worsened teacher shortages. Abolishing fees also removed the money schools had used to pay PTA-hired teachers. The governor approved recruitment, which his website describes as 7,000 teachers. A commentary one year in reported that post-primary recruitment was paused during COVID-19 and that primary-school gaps remained (UNVERIFIED as to final numbers). The World Bank provided a ₦3.5 billion grant to renovate 105 public primary schools under its Better Education Service Delivery for All programme. That project is co-designed and co-funded by external partners and cannot be credited wholly to the state.

Federal education policy covers universities, student loans and UBEC transfers. His manifesto proposes a National Foundational Learning Guarantee: at least 50 per cent of Primary Three pupils meeting literacy standards and 65 per cent meeting numeracy standards within three years, and a 25 per cent cut in the gap between the best- and worst-performing states (PROMISE). ANALYSIS: primary schooling is run mainly by states and local governments, so a federal guarantee would depend on state cooperation and reliable learning data.
strengths: Fee abolition delivered on day one as promised
Quantified national learning targets
limitations: Teacher shortages followed the enrolment increase
No independent learning-outcome data for Oyo found
unknowns: Cost of the foundational learning guarantee

healthcare.summary: Oyo pursued a one-functional-PHC-per-ward policy linked to federal Basic Health Care Provision Fund money. Critics say other clinics were neglected. He proposes a national essential primary-care guarantee.
healthcare.analysis:
State governments run primary and secondary health facilities. Oyo has more than 760 primary health centres. Through a one-facility-per-ward policy, 351 of them, one in each ward, receive money from the federal Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) (FACT, per TheCable's reporting). TheCable's field reporting describes improved maternal care at some funded facilities. A Leadership report argues the policy concentrates resources in the selected centres and leaves other rural clinics behind, which could harm rural residents (ANALYSIS by the outlet). The available figures on how many centres were renovated come from government statements or state-linked outlets, and they differ from one another, so this research does not treat any single completion figure as verified. BHCPF is a federal statutory fund. Improvements at funded PHCs therefore reflect shared federal-state financing and are not solely a state achievement.

As a presidential plan, his manifesto proposes an essential primary-care guarantee specifying the services, medicines, staff and referral arrangements a participating facility must provide. It also proposes expanded health insurance for poor and vulnerable people, focused on maternal care, immunisation and preventable disease (PROMISE). ANALYSIS: the plan follows the Oyo ward model, but the coverage reviewed gives no cost, staffing target or timeline.
strengths: Clear primary-care focus consistent with his state record
Use of national BHCPF channel
limitations: Completion figures for PHC upgrades are government-sourced and inconsistent
Critics report neglect of non-selected facilities
unknowns: Oyo health budget share and release rates

infrastructure.summary: The Ibadan Circular Road, conceived in 2002, was re-awarded under Makinde. Bridges on the first wing were reported largely complete in 2023, but the road was still unfinished and a land-acquisition dispute led to a corridor reduction in 2025.
infrastructure.analysis:
The Ibadan Circular Road is a multi-administration project. It was envisioned under Governor Lam Adesina in 2002 and surveyed under Rashidi Ladoja in 2005. Abiola Ajimobi revived it in 2017 as a build-operate-transfer PPP with the ENL Consortium, which had completed about 5.5 per cent when Makinde halted the work in October 2019 (RECORD). Litigation followed. Makinde's government awarded completion of the 110 km ring for ₦138.2 billion; the APC opposition criticised that cost. In March 2022, Craneburg Construction was engaged on the 32.2 km east wing. In July 2023 the contractor's engineer reported four of six bridges complete and two at 90 per cent. He said the deadline covered bridges and interchanges, not the road itself, and flooding was a problem. Status: partially-completed, with no independently verified overall completion figure found.

In November 2025, after protests by corridor residents, the government reduced land acquisition from 500 m to 150 m in developed areas. The 500 m width still applies in undeveloped areas. Officials denied allocating corridor land to private developers and said compensation would be paid in appropriate cases. They added that much of the land had been compensated under Ladoja, and that Ajimobi, not Makinde, had widened the corridor (RECORD; DISPUTED by residents). ANALYSIS: the project shows long-cycle state infrastructure where credit and delay are shared across administrations.
strengths: Revived a long-stalled ring-road project with visible bridge works
Responded to resident protests by narrowing the corridor
limitations: Overall road not complete after seven years
Land-acquisition dispute and contested compensation
Contract cost criticised by opposition
unknowns: Current verified completion percentage of the full 110 km
Total paid to contractors to date

power.summary: Oyo was among the first states to take over regulation of its electricity market under the Electricity Act 2023. As of 2026 the market was still in transition. He proposes a coordinated national-state electricity market.
power.analysis:
The Electricity Act 2023 lets states regulate their own intrastate electricity markets. Oyo passed its State Electricity Regulatory Commission law in 2024. In August 2024, NERC transferred regulatory oversight of Oyo's market to the state regulator (RECORD/FACT). NERC's order directed the Ibadan Electricity Distribution Company (IBEDC) to set up a subsidiary within 60 days to take over its Oyo franchise and obtain a licence from the state regulator. It also made tariffs approved by the state commission the exclusive end-user tariffs in Oyo. In February 2026, NERC hosted the Oyo commission to coordinate the transition. Oyo officials have reported investor interest. This research found no evidence that the IBEDC subsidiary has been licensed, no published state tariff schedule, and no change in supply hours for residents. The transfer is a regulatory step, not yet a measured improvement in power supply.

For the presidency, the manifesto proposes a coordinated national and state electricity market in which states take more responsibility for intrastate distribution and local supply (PROMISE). ANALYSIS: this extends a reform already under way under the 2023 Act. Grid transmission, gas supply and generation remain federal and private-sector matters that the plan addresses only in outline. His professional background is in power and oil-and-gas engineering.
strengths: Early mover on state electricity market under the 2023 Act
Relevant engineering background
limitations: No measured supply or tariff outcomes yet
National generation/transmission/gas plans not detailed in sources reviewed
unknowns: Status of IBEDC Oyo subsidiary licensing

jobs.summary: His jobs record rests mainly on agribusiness programmes such as the Fasola hub, and the job figures come from the government. He proposes crop-specific value-chain plans but has published no national jobs target.
jobs.analysis:
Employment outcomes are shaped largely by national macroeconomic conditions. A state can mainly influence agriculture, MSME support and investment promotion. The Oyo government reports that the Fasola Industrial Hub attracted more than ₦10 billion in private investment and created 1,500 direct and indirect jobs (UNVERIFIED: government figure). A Premium Times analysis of his manifesto cites about ₦20 billion in private investment, 16 companies and training for over 5,000 young people. The two sets of figures differ, and no independent audit of job creation was found. The state also runs youth agribusiness training and credit schemes with private banks. No current Oyo unemployment rate was found, because NBS state-level labour data is irregular.

The manifesto treats jobs as an outcome of lower production costs. It proposes delivery plans for priority crops (rice, maize, cassava, beans and tomatoes) covering inputs, financing, storage, processing and markets. Government would provide shared infrastructure and private investors would produce and employ (PROMISE). It also proposes a 'Tell Government Once' reform of 20 high-volume federal business processes in year one. ANALYSIS: the approach is mechanism-based but sets no job-creation target, so delivery would be hard to measure.
strengths: Concrete agribusiness hub model with private investment
Business-process reform with a numeric year-one target
limitations: Job figures are government-reported and inconsistent
No national employment target

finance.summary: Under Makinde, IGR and reported budget performance rose. DMO-based data show debt stock falling to December 2025, while state budget reports show heavy new borrowing in 2025-2026, and the two have not been reconciled. BudgIT ranked Oyo low on fiscal transparency in Q4 2024.
finance.analysis:
Oyo's budget grew from a ₦434.2 billion proposal for 2024 to a ₦684.1 billion 2025 appropriation, about half of it capital spending (FACT). The budget commissioner said budget performance improved from 57.4 per cent in 2019 to 71.4 per cent in 2024. These are the state's own figures; audited outturns were not reviewed. An analysis of DMO data by intelpoint reports external debt falling from about $137 million in June 2019 to $88 million in December 2025. The same analysis reports domestic debt falling from ₦99 billion to ₦77 billion over that period, after peaking at about ₦162 billion in 2022-2023 (FACT, secondary analysis of DMO data).

Sahara Reporters, citing the state's Q1 2026 budget performance document, reports borrowing of ₦62 billion in 2024, ₦219 billion in 2025 and ₦164.8 billion in January-March 2026, more than six times IGR in that quarter. It also reports a lawmaker's allegation that a ₦300 billion loan was approved during a legislative recess (UNVERIFIED; no government response reported). ANALYSIS: gross borrowing flows, short-term facilities and rollovers can differ from year-end stock, so these figures do not necessarily contradict each other, but they have not been reconciled. In its Q4 2024 fiscal transparency ranking, BudgIT placed Oyo among the lowest-scoring states. The Q1 2026 drawdown came as the state was moving into an election year.
strengths: Rising IGR and reported budget-performance improvement
DMO-based debt stock lower in December 2025 than June 2019
limitations: Large reported borrowing in 2025-Q1 2026
Low BudgIT transparency score in Q4 2024
Legislator's allegation about recess loan approval unresolved
unknowns: Primary DMO figures for Oyo at 31 Dec 2025 and 30 June 2026
Purpose and terms of the 2025-2026 loans

metrics.label: Reported borrowing
metrics.note: Sahara Reporters citing state budget performance document

leadership.summary: He has run a state for two terms and built a cross-party PDP-APM arrangement, but the Supreme Court found he had dissolved elected councils unlawfully. He proposes a 'transitional government of national unity'.
leadership.analysis:
On assuming office in 2019, Makinde dissolved elected chairmen and councillors in Oyo's 33 local governments and 35 development areas, although a High Court had restrained the dissolution. In May 2021, the Supreme Court held this unconstitutional and said he had acted in contemptuous disregard of the High Court judgment. The councils were reinstated five days before their tenure ended, with salaries ordered paid. Makinde said he would comply (RECORD). In 2023, the Court of Appeal affirmed an order to pay ₦3.4 billion in outstanding entitlements to the former council officials.

His 2026 candidacy rests on an unusual arrangement: a sitting PDP governor running as the APM candidate under an undisclosed PDP-APM memorandum of understanding. Premium Times linked the arrangement to the PDP's leadership crisis (RECORD/ANALYSIS). He proposes a transitional government of national unity from 29 May 2027, a 100-day delivery plan and quarterly public scorecards (PROMISE). ANALYSIS: the scorecards would give voters a way to check delivery. Running the presidency would require coalition management across parties and a legislature where the APM has little presence, and his state record offers no comparable test.
strengths: Two full terms of state executive experience
Pledged quarterly public scorecards
limitations: Supreme Court ruling against unlawful council dissolution
Untested coalition model at national level
unknowns: Composition of proposed government of national unity

integrity.summary: He publicly declared his assets in 2019. A court set aside an EFCC records request as overbroad, a civil-society petition over Bodija explosion funds was denied by the state, and he faced adverse rulings over the council dissolution. No criminal charge was found.
integrity.analysis:
In July 2019, Makinde made public his Code of Conduct Bureau declaration, reporting assets worth about ₦48.15 billion, mainly company holdings. He said the publication fulfilled a campaign pledge (RECORD).

On 2 June 2025, the EFCC wrote to the state Accountant-General requesting all contracts and payments to contractors from 2021. The state sued after, it says, the EFCC declined to identify specific targets. In July 2026, Justice Nkeonye Maha of the Federal High Court, Ibadan, set aside the request as a speculative 'fishing expedition' outside Section 38 of the EFCC Act (legalStatus: judgment). The ruling concerned the scope of the request. It did not find for or against any wrongdoing, and no appeal was reported.

In January 2026, HEDA petitioned the EFCC alleging misapplication of ₦30 billion in federal intervention funds released after the January 2024 Bodija explosion. The state replied that the ₦30 billion was untouched, that a ₦20 billion balance had not been released, and that it had spent its own funds on recovery (legalStatus: allegation, denied). Separately, courts ruled against his government over the 2019 dissolution of local councils (legalStatus: judgment). ANALYSIS: these are civil and constitutional rulings plus an unproven allegation. No criminal charge or conviction against him was found.
strengths: Voluntary public asset declaration
No criminal charges found
limitations: Adverse Supreme Court and Court of Appeal rulings on council dissolution
Unresolved civil-society allegation about Bodija funds
unknowns: Whether the EFCC appealed the July 2026 judgment
Any EFCC action on the HEDA petition

experience.summary: He has served seven-plus years as governor of a large state, after two decades as an engineer and founder of an oil, gas and power firm. He has no federal executive or legislative experience.
experience.analysis:
Makinde graduated in electrical engineering from the University of Lagos in 1990. He spent about five years with international oil and gas firms, then founded Makon Engineering and Technical Services in 1997. It grew into a group active in oil and gas and power. A 2024 profile says he resigned in 2018 (FACT). He lost Oyo governorship bids before winning in 2019 with 515,621 votes and was re-elected in 2023 with 563,756 votes (FACT). Previous bids are not detailed in the sources reviewed.

As governor he has managed annual budgets that reached ₦684 billion in 2025. He has also dealt with a mass-casualty explosion in Ibadan, a mass school abduction, a contested land-acquisition programme, and one of the first state takeovers of electricity regulation. ANALYSIS: this is substantial sub-national executive experience in exactly the areas where his manifesto draws on Oyo models: primary health care, agribusiness hubs and state electricity markets. He has not held federal office, commanded federal security agencies, managed foreign relations, or worked with the National Assembly from the executive side. Those are core presidential functions where his record cannot be directly tested. The scale gap between a state budget and the federal budget is also material.
strengths: Two terms as governor
Private-sector founder in energy
Experience of crisis management at state level
limitations: No federal or foreign-policy experience
No legislative experience
unknowns: Independent assessment of Makon Group performance

vision.summary: 'The Reset Agenda' has four pillars, a three-plus-one-year delivery structure and several quantified targets. Full costing and the full text were not found.
strengths: Quantified targets and deadlines
Built-in public scorecard mechanism
limitations: Costing not published in sources reviewed
Heavy dependence on constitutional amendments
unknowns: Revenue assumptions behind the deficit target

foreign.summary: No foreign-policy platform was found. His relevant record is limited to state-level development-partner projects such as a World Bank education grant.
foreign.analysis: Foreign policy is a federal power, so a governor's record touches it only through development-partner relationships. Oyo under Makinde implemented World Bank-assisted programmes, including a ₦3.5 billion grant for 105 primary schools. The press coverage of his manifesto reviewed for this research does not mention foreign policy, ECOWAS, trade agreements or diaspora policy. His running mate's security background may bear on regional security cooperation, but no stated position was found.
limitations: No published foreign-policy positions found
unknowns: Positions on ECOWAS, AU, Sahel states and trade
missing: Foreign-policy chapter of the Reset Agenda, if any
Statements on ECOWAS and the Sahel juntas
Positions on trade agreements (AfCFTA) and foreign investment policy

humanImpact.summary: Fee abolition lowered household school costs. Residents were affected by the circular-road land acquisition and by insecurity, while food inflation was mainly national in origin.
humanImpact.analysis:
The clearest documented household effect of his tenure is the 2019 abolition of the ₦3,000 secondary-school levy and other in-school fees. It cut direct costs for families using public schools, though external exam fees remained (RECORD). On the other side, residents along the Ibadan Circular Road corridor protested in 2025 over demolition markings and land acquisition. The government narrowed the corridor to 150 m in developed areas and said it would pay compensation in appropriate cases. How many households were finally affected or compensated is not documented in the sources reviewed (UNVERIFIED).

Insecurity directly harmed residents. The May 2026 Oriire abduction took schoolchildren and teachers from rural communities. The governor reported that nearly 200 Amotekun operatives had died over six years. Food inflation in Oyo reached 34.41 per cent in March 2025. ANALYSIS: that was mainly the result of national subsidy removal, exchange-rate changes and insecurity in food-producing areas, not of state policy. The state says its transport-support programmes eased costs, and he proposes to scale them nationally, but no independent evaluation was found.
strengths: Direct cost relief through fee abolition
limitations: Displacement and compensation disputes on the circular road
No independent evaluation of state transport and welfare programmes
unknowns: Number of households affected by circular-road acquisition

promises.summary: Several 2019 state promises were delivered visibly, including fee abolition and asset declaration. His presidential promises are specific and time-bound but depend on legislation.
promises.analysis:
Two promises from his 2019 governorship campaign are well documented: abolishing secondary-school fees, done on inauguration day, and publicly declaring his assets, done in July 2019 (RECORD). His teacher-recruitment commitment was only partly implemented on the available evidence. The circular road, revived under his administration, remains incomplete (RECORD).

As a presidential candidate he is an aspirant for that office. His promises are therefore judged on specificity, not delivery. The Reset Agenda attaches deadlines to most commitments: refinery assessments in six months and decisions in 12; a delivery plan in 100 days; state police by the end of year three; deficit and debt-service targets by the end of year three; and foundational learning targets within three years. It also commits to quarterly public scorecards rating each promise as completed, on track, delayed or not achieved (PROMISE). ANALYSIS: by Nigerian campaign standards this is a high degree of specificity. The main feasibility risks are constitutional amendments, oil-revenue assumptions behind the Domestic Energy Value Credit, and the absence of published costs. Some reports describe the timeline as four years and others as three years plus consolidation. That difference is a matter of framing, not substance.
strengths: Delivered high-visibility 2019 promises
Time-bound presidential commitments with a scorecard
limitations: Some 2019 promises only partly delivered
Presidential promises lack published costing
unknowns: Full 2019 promise list and an independent tracker of delivery

test.answer: Yes. The manifesto names the drivers it targets: production costs, insecurity, power, storage losses and financing costs, plus a 67.22% debt-service ratio and learning gaps.
Largely. Refinery paths, a phased state-police timeline, learning targets and fiscal ratios are specific. Housing and foreign policy are not.
Partly. Several items draw on Oyo pilots (ward PHCs, Fasola hub, state electricity market), but independent evaluations of those pilots were not found.
Unclear. The plan relies on redirecting existing spending and on fiscal limits; costing of the energy credit and other items was not published in the sources reviewed.
Partly. Three years for state police and refinery restructuring is ambitious given that constitutional amendments are needed.
Partly. Refineries, fiscal policy and federal security fall within presidential authority. Basic education, state police and devolution depend on states and constitutional change.
Yes. State police, devolution and council reorganisation need constitutional amendments, and the fiscal measures need appropriation.
Partly. Coverage notes the need for amendments and federal-state cooperation, but no formal risk section was found.
Partly. The running mate (a former SSS Director-General) is known; no cabinet or delivery-unit team has been announced.
Yes, at state level: two terms as governor, with fee abolition, state electricity regulation and ward PHC policies. There is no federal execution record.
